title: Two Sum
statement: Given an unsorted array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Exactly one answer exists and you may not use the same element twice.

nearMiss.why: The array is unsorted and you must return original indices; sorting first costs O(n log n) and loses the indices unless you carry them along.
Binary search needs sorted data; sorting breaks the index answer and still costs O(n log n).
The two numbers need not be next to each other, so there is no contiguous window to slide.

trigger.answer: two numbers that add up to the target
trigger.why: A pair that sums to a target means: for each x, have I already seen target − x? That is a complement lookup in a hash map.

ds.answer: HashMap<Integer, Integer> (value → index)

wrong.why: A set says the complement exists but not WHERE; the answer needs its index.
Works, but O(log n) per operation for no benefit: you never need ordering.

ds.why: You need the complement's index in O(1), so map value → index.

invariant.answer: Before checking index i, the map holds every value at indices 0..i−1 with its index.
wrong: The map holds every value in the array before the loop starts.
The map holds only values smaller than the target.
The map is sorted by value so the complement can be binary searched.
invariant.why: Checking before inserting guarantees the partner comes from an earlier index, so an element never pairs with itself.

time.why: One pass with O(1) average map operations.

space.why: The map can hold up to n entries.

wrong: Two pointers only works on arrays of positive numbers.
Two pointers can find triplets but not pairs.
Two pointers needs more memory than a hash map.

approach: Walk once; for each value look up target − value in a map of value → index seen so far. If present return both indices, otherwise store the current value.

twists.change: The array is sorted, and you may only use O(1) extra space.
twists.statement: Given an integer array sorted in ascending order and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target, using O(1) extra space.
twists.ds: Two int indices lo and hi

nearMiss.why: The complement map still works, but it's O(n) space and ignores the sorted order you were given.
The two numbers needn't be adjacent; there's no window.
It's a sum of exactly two elements, not of a range.

twists.why: Sorted order tells you which end to move: sum too small ⇒ lo++, too big ⇒ hi−−.
twists.approach: lo = 0, hi = n − 1; move the pointer that fixes the sum until it equals target.

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Given a list of strings, group together the words that are anagrams of each other (same letters in a different order) and return the groups in any order.

nearMiss.why: A trie groups words by shared prefix, but anagrams share letters, not prefixes.
Comparing every pair of words is O(n² · k); there is no ordering to converge on.
Each word is compared as a whole, not as a contiguous window inside one longer string.

wrong: return the groups in any order
trigger.why: 'Group items that share a property' → compute a canonical key for each item and bucket by it in a hash map.

ds.answer: HashMap<String, List<String>> keyed by sorted letters or a 26-count signature
ds.why: The key identifies the group and the value collects its members; computeIfAbsent builds the buckets in one pass.

invariant.answer: All words with the same canonical key are in the same bucket, and no bucket mixes keys.
wrong: Words are grouped by their first letter.
The map never holds more than 26 keys.
invariant.why: Anagrams produce identical keys; non-anagrams can't, so key equality is exactly group membership.

time.answer: O(n · k log k) with sorted keys (O(n · k) with count keys)
time.why: n words, each sorted in O(k log k) (or counted in O(k)); map operations are O(k) to hash the key.

space.why: Every word is stored once in a bucket, plus its key.

wrong: A trie can't store lowercase strings.
A trie needs every word to have the same length.

approach: For each word build a key (sorted characters, or the 26 letter counts joined into a string) and append the word to map[key]. Return the map's values.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement: Given an unsorted array of integers, return the length of the longest run of consecutive values (like 4, 5, 6, 7) that appear anywhere in the array. Your algorithm must run in O(n) time.

nearMiss.why: The values are consecutive numbers, not consecutive positions; they can be scattered anywhere in the array.
Sorting (or binary searching) costs O(n log n), which breaks the O(n) requirement.
The sequence lives in value space, not index order, so there is no left-to-right recurrence over the array.

wrong: return the length of the longest run
trigger.why: O(n) rules out sorting. You need O(1) 'is x − 1 / x + 1 present?' checks, which is a hash set.

ds.answer: HashSet<Integer> of all values

wrong.why: Sorted, but O(log n) per operation, so O(n log n) overall.

wrong: int[] sorted copy of the array
ds.why: Only membership matters, so a set is enough.

invariant.answer: You only start counting from x when x − 1 is NOT in the set, so each run is walked once from its start.
wrong: You count upward from every x in the set.
The set stays sorted so neighbours are adjacent.
The set holds only values inside the current run.
invariant.why: Starting only at run starts makes the total walking O(n) even though there is a nested loop.

time.why: Each value is inserted once and visited at most twice (once as a candidate start, once while walking a run).

space.why: The set stores every distinct value.

wrong: A sliding window can only find runs of exactly length k.
Sliding windows only work on strings, not integers.
The window would need O(n²) memory.

approach: Put all values in a HashSet. For each x where x − 1 is absent (a run start), count x + 1, x + 2, … while present; track the longest run.

title: 3Sum
statement: Given an integer array, return all unique triplets [a, b, c] from different positions with a + b + c = 0. The result must not contain duplicate triplets.

nearMiss.why: Generating every 3-element combination is O(n³); sorting lets the sum constraint prune pairs in O(n) per fixed element.
Fixing two numbers and binary searching the third is O(n² log n); two pointers removes the log factor.
The three numbers need not be contiguous, so there is no window.

trigger.why: A fixed-sum condition on a pair or triplet, plus freedom to sort, is the two-pointer signal: fix one, then converge on the pair.

ds.answer: The sorted int[] itself with index pointers; List<List<Integer>> for results

wrong.why: Works, but hides the real fix (skip equal neighbours after sorting) and costs extra space.

ds.why: After sorting, pointers plus skipping equal neighbours handle both the search and the de-duplication.

invariant.answer: For a fixed i, every pair outside [lo, hi] has been ruled out: if the sum is too small only lo++ can help, if too big only hi--.
wrong: lo and hi always point at equal values.
The sum nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi] never decreases.
Every value between lo and hi is negative.
invariant.why: Sorted order makes the move direction forced, so no valid pair is skipped.

time.why: Sorting is O(n log n); for each i the inner two-pointer scan is O(n).

space.answer: O(1) extra (ignoring the output and the sort)
space.why: Only pointers; Java's primitive sort uses O(log n) stack.

wrong: Backtracking can't produce triplets, only permutations.
Backtracking needs the input to be sorted.

approach: Sort. For each i (skipping duplicate values of nums[i]) run lo = i + 1, hi = n − 1 towards each other: sum < 0 → lo++, > 0 → hi--, = 0 → record, then skip duplicates on both sides.

title: Container With Most Water
statement: Given the heights of n vertical lines at positions 0..n−1, pick two lines that together with the x-axis hold the most water. Return that maximum area (width × the shorter height).

nearMiss.why: Monotonic stacks answer 'next greater' for each element; here the best pair can be far apart and depends on width as well as height.
There are no overlapping subproblems; the answer is one pair found by discarding the shorter side each step.
The area is between two chosen lines, not over a window with a validity rule; you start at full width and shrink from the outside.

trigger.why: Choosing the best PAIR on an ordered line, where moving the shorter end is the only move that can help, is converging two pointers.

ds.answer: Two int indices (lo, hi) on the heights array
ds.why: Nothing else is needed: each step discards one line.

invariant.answer: Any container using the shorter of height[lo] and height[hi] with a narrower width can't beat the current area, so that line can be discarded.
wrong: The area increases every time a pointer moves.
All lines between lo and hi are shorter than both ends.
invariant.why: Width only shrinks, so keeping the shorter line can never give a larger area.

time.why: Each step moves one pointer inward.

space.why: Two indices and a best value.

wrong: Monotonic stacks only work on sorted arrays.
A stack needs all heights to be distinct.

approach: lo = 0, hi = n − 1; area = (hi − lo) · min(h[lo], h[hi]); move the pointer at the shorter line inward; keep the max.

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: Given an elevation map as an array of non-negative bar heights (each bar has width 1), compute how much rain water is trapped between the bars after it rains.

nearMiss.why: There is no window validity rule; water above each bar depends on the tallest bars anywhere to its left AND right.
A heap is used for the 2D version (Trapping Rain Water II); in 1D the left and right maxima are enough.
Kadane tracks a best running subarray sum; water per bar depends on maxima on both sides, not a running sum.

trigger.why: Water above a bar = min(max left, max right) − height. Needing both sides' maxima → two pointers from both ends (or precomputed left/right max arrays).

ds.answer: Two int indices plus leftMax and rightMax scalars
ds.why: The two-pointer version settles one bar per step using only the two running maxima.

invariant.answer: If leftMax < rightMax, the water at lo is decided by leftMax (the right side is guaranteed at least as tall), so lo can be settled and advanced.
wrong: leftMax and rightMax are always equal.
Water at each bar equals the global max height minus the bar's height.
lo only moves when height[lo] is greater than height[hi].
invariant.why: The smaller of the two maxima is the binding wall for that side.

time.why: Each bar is settled once.

space.why: Four scalars. (The prefix-max version uses O(n); the stack version O(n).)

wrong: Sliding windows can't be used on arrays of heights.
The window would need to be sorted first.
A sliding window here would be O(n²).

approach: lo, hi from both ends with leftMax, rightMax. Move the side with the smaller max: water += thatMax − height there. Equivalent: precompute leftMax[] and rightMax[] and sum min(...) − height.

twists.change: The heights form a 2-D grid instead of a line.
twists.statement: Given an m × n grid of block heights, compute how much rain water the whole 2-D elevation map can hold after raining.
twists.trigger: m × n grid of block heights
twists.ds: PriorityQueue<int[]> of {height, r, c} seeded with the border, plus boolean[][] visited

nearMiss.why: In 1-D the lower of two walls bounds the water; in 2-D water can escape in any direction, so you need the lowest point of the whole boundary.
Row and column max sweeps don't capture leaks around corners.
Plain BFS has no priority; you must always grow from the lowest boundary cell.

twists.why: Water level is set by the lowest wall around a basin ⇒ grow inwards from the border with a min-heap (Dijkstra-like on max height).
twists.approach: Push all border cells. Poll the lowest; for each unvisited neighbour: water += max(0, h − nh); push (max(h, nh), neighbour).

title: Move Zeroes
statement: Move all 0s in an integer array to the end while keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements. Do it in place without making a copy of the array.

nearMiss.why: Dutch-flag / Hoare partitioning swaps from both ends and does not preserve the relative order of the non-zero elements.
Collecting non-zeros in a stack or list uses O(n) extra space, which 'in place' rules out.
There is no contiguous range to optimise; you are compacting elements.

trigger.answer: in place without making a copy
trigger.why: In-place compaction (keep some elements, push others to the back) is the same-direction read/write pointer pattern.

ds.answer: One write index and one read index on the same int[]
ds.why: Both pointers live on the input; nothing else is needed.

invariant.answer: nums[0..write) holds the non-zero elements seen so far, in their original order.
wrong: nums[write..n) holds only zeros at every step.
read and write are always equal.
Every swap moves a zero to its final position.
invariant.why: write only advances when a non-zero is placed, so the prefix is exactly the compacted non-zeros.

time.why: One pass of the read pointer.

space.why: Two indices.

wrong: Partitioning requires the array to be sorted.
Partitioning can't be done in place.
Partitioning only works for arrays of 0s, 1s and 2s.

approach: write = 0; for each read, if nums[read] != 0 swap nums[write] and nums[read], then write++. Non-zeros keep their order; zeros end at the back.

title: Next Permutation
statement: Rearrange an array of integers into the next lexicographically greater permutation of its values, in place. If it is already the largest permutation, rearrange it into ascending order.

nearMiss.why: Listing permutations in order is O(n! · n); you need only the next one, in place.
There is no top-k selection; the change is confined to the suffix after a pivot.
No overlapping subproblems; one right-to-left scan finds the pivot.

trigger.why: Next permutation = scan from the right for the first descent (pivot), swap it with the smallest larger value to its right, then reverse the suffix with two pointers.

ds.answer: Index variables on the int[] (pivot scan, swap, then reverse the suffix)
ds.why: Everything happens in the array with a few indices.

invariant.answer: The suffix right of the pivot is in non-increasing order, so it is already the largest arrangement of those values.
wrong: The prefix left of the pivot is sorted ascending.
The pivot is always the largest element.
After the swap the suffix is already ascending.
invariant.why: That is why the pivot must change, and why reversing the (still descending) suffix gives the smallest continuation.

time.why: At most two right-to-left scans and one reversal.

space.why: In place with a few indices.

wrong: Backtracking can't produce permutations in lexicographic order.
Backtracking only works on sorted input.

approach: From the right find i with nums[i] < nums[i + 1]. If found, from the right find j with nums[j] > nums[i] and swap. Reverse nums[i + 1..]. (No such i ⇒ reverse the whole array.)

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string, return the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated characters.

nearMiss.why: Converging pointers from both ends don't fit: a valid substring is grown and shrunk in the same direction.
Enumerating substrings is O(n²) or worse; the 'no repeats' rule is monotonic, so one window pass is O(n).
There is no sum to take differences of; the rule is about character repeats inside the window.

trigger.why: Longest/shortest + substring (contiguous) + a rule that only breaks as you grow → sliding window.

ds.answer: int[128] (or HashMap<Character, Integer>) of last-seen index, plus left/right indices
ds.why: Last-seen positions let the left edge jump past a repeat in O(1).

invariant.answer: s[left..right] never contains a repeated character.
wrong: left only moves when right reaches the end.
The window always contains every distinct character seen so far.
right − left is always the best length so far.
invariant.why: Whenever s[right] repeats inside the window, left jumps just past the earlier copy.

time.why: right moves n times and left only ever moves forward.

space.why: One entry per distinct character, bounded by the alphabet (e.g. 128).

wrong: Two pointers can't be used on strings.
Two pointers needs a target sum.
Two pointers would use O(n) extra space.

approach: Expand right; if s[right] was last seen at index ≥ left, move left to lastSeen + 1. Update lastSeen and best = max(best, right − left + 1).

twists.change: The characters no longer need to be contiguous.
twists.statement: Given a string, return the length of the longest subsequence (characters in order, not necessarily adjacent) in which no character repeats.

nearMiss.why: A window only covers contiguous substrings; a subsequence can skip any repeats, so no window is needed.
No choices interact: take one copy of every distinct character.
Enumerating subsequences is exponential for a question with a counting answer.

twists.why: If you can skip characters, keep the first copy of each distinct one: the answer is the number of distinct characters.
twists.approach: Add every character to a set; return its size.

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement: Given strings s and t, return the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t (including duplicates). Return an empty string if no such substring exists.

nearMiss.why: Two strings suggest a 2D table, but t is only a multiset of required counts and s is scanned once.
Converging from both ends can't work; the window must grow and shrink in one direction to try every right edge.
Per-character prefix counts can test a window in O(alphabet), but trying every window is still O(n²).

trigger.why: Shortest contiguous substring that satisfies a coverage rule → variable sliding window that shrinks while still valid.

ds.answer: int[128] required counts for t plus a 'missing' counter; left/right indices on s

wrong.why: A set loses duplicate counts, and t may contain repeated characters.

ds.why: Counts plus one 'missing' number make the validity check O(1).

invariant.answer: missing == 0 exactly when s[left..right] covers every required character count of t.
wrong: The window always has the same length as t.
Every character in the window belongs to t.
left never passes the first occurrence of t's first character.
invariant.why: missing drops only when a still-needed character enters and rises when one leaves.

time.why: Counting t once; each index of s enters and leaves the window once.

space.answer: O(alphabet), i.e. O(1) for fixed ASCII
wrong: O(|s| + |t|) for a copy of both
space.why: Only the count array.

wrong: A DP table would need t to be sorted.
DP only works when s and t have equal length.

approach: Count t. Expand right, decrementing need; when missing hits 0, shrink left while still valid, recording the shortest window, then step past validity and continue.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
statement: Given an uppercase string and an integer k, you may change at most k characters. Return the length of the longest substring that can be made of one repeated letter.

nearMiss.why: A DP over positions with 'changes used' is O(n · k); the window gives O(n) because validity is monotonic.
Changing the globally least frequent letters ignores contiguity; the k changes must all fall inside one substring.
Trying every set of k changes is exponential.

trigger.why: 'At most k' + longest contiguous substring = variable sliding window, valid while windowLength − topCount ≤ k.

ds.answer: int[26] counts in the window plus maxCount and left/right indices
wrong: PriorityQueue<Integer> of counts rebuilt each step
ds.why: Letter counts and the best single-letter count decide validity in O(1).

invariant.answer: The window satisfies windowLength − maxCount ≤ k: the non-majority letters can all be replaced.
wrong: The window contains at most k distinct letters.
The window contains exactly k replaced letters.
maxCount always equals the true maximum count in the current window.
invariant.why: maxCount may be stale (it never decreases) and that is fine: the answer only grows when a larger maxCount appears.

time.why: Each index enters and leaves once; updates are O(1).

space.why: Fixed alphabet.

wrong: DP would need k to be zero.
DP requires the string to be sorted.

approach: Expand right, update counts and maxCount; while (right − left + 1) − maxCount > k, decrement count[s[left]] and left++. Best is the largest window length.

title: Subarray Product Less Than K
statement: Given an array of positive integers and an integer k, count the contiguous subarrays whose product is strictly less than k.

nearMiss.why: Prefix + hash map finds EXACT targets; this asks for 'less than', and positivity makes the window monotonic.
Kadane finds a maximum, not a count of subarrays under a bound.
No ordering by size is needed; it is a count over contiguous ranges.

trigger.why: Positivity makes the window monotonic: growing can only raise the product, shrinking only lowers it. With 'contiguous', that is sliding window.

ds.answer: Two int indices and a running long product
ds.why: Multiply in on the right, divide out on the left.

invariant.answer: After shrinking, the product of nums[left..right] is < k, so every subarray ending at right that starts in [left, right] counts: right − left + 1 of them.
wrong: The window product is always exactly k − 1.
left and right always move together.
The window never contains duplicate values.
invariant.why: Any sub-window of a valid window is also valid (all numbers ≥ 1).

time.why: Each index enters and leaves once.

space.why: A product and two indices.

wrong: Prefix sums can't be used with multiplication at all.
Prefix sums need the array sorted.
Prefix sums only work when k is zero.

approach: If k ≤ 1 return 0. Expand right multiplying; while product ≥ k divide out nums[left++]; add right − left + 1.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement: Given an array and a window size k that slides one step at a time from left to right, return the maximum value in each window position.

nearMiss.why: A max-heap works with lazy deletion of out-of-window entries, but it is O(n log k); the deque gives O(n).
A next-greater stack never expires items from its far end; the window also needs removal from the front.
Prefix arrays answer range SUMS in O(1), not range maximums (max has no inverse to subtract).

trigger.answer: maximum value in each window position
wrong: slides one step at a time
trigger.why: Max (or min) of every sliding window → keep a monotonic deque of candidates.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<Integer> of indices with decreasing values

wrong.why: O(n log k), and values alone can't tell you when an entry left the window.

ds.why: Indices let you expire the front; decreasing values keep the max at the front.

invariant.answer: Deque indices lie inside the current window and their values decrease from front to back, so the front is the max.
wrong: The deque holds exactly k indices at all times.
The deque is sorted ascending so the max is at the back.
Every element of the window is in the deque.
invariant.why: A smaller element behind a larger, newer one can never be a window max again, so it is dropped.

time.why: Every index is pushed and popped at most once.

space.why: The deque never holds more than one window's worth of indices (output not counted).

wrong: A heap would return the minimum, not the maximum.

approach: For each i: pop back while nums[back] ≤ nums[i]; push i; pop front if it is ≤ i − k; once i ≥ k − 1 record nums[front].

twists.change: Report each window's sum instead of its maximum.
twists.statement: Given an integer array and a window size k, return the sum of every contiguous window of size k.
twists.trigger: the sum of every contiguous window

nearMiss.why: The deque exists to find a window's max/min; a sum is updated by adding the new value and subtracting the old.
No ordering is needed for sums.
The window is a fixed size; there's nothing to converge on.

twists.why: Sums are invertible: add the entering element and subtract the leaving one.
twists.approach: sum += a[i]; if i ≥ k sum −= a[i − k]; if i ≥ k − 1 output sum.

title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
statement: Given an integer array whose values may be negative and an integer k, return the length of the shortest non-empty contiguous subarray with sum at least k, or −1 if none exists.

nearMiss.why: With negative numbers, shrinking the window doesn't reliably lower the sum, so the plain two-index window breaks.
'Some subarray of length L has sum ≥ k' is not monotonic in L when negatives exist, so the length can't be binary searched.
Kadane maximises a sum; this minimises length subject to a sum threshold.

trigger.why: Shortest subarray with sum ≥ k would be sliding window, except negatives break it. That twist leads to prefix sums plus a monotonic deque of candidate starts.

ds.answer: long[] prefix sums + ArrayDeque<Integer> of indices with increasing prefix values

wrong.why: A heap version works in O(n log n); the deque is O(n).

ds.why: Candidate start indices kept in increasing prefix order.

invariant.answer: Deque indices have strictly increasing prefix sums; an index whose prefix is ≥ a later one's can never be the best start and is dropped.
wrong: The deque holds the last k indices.
Prefix sums in the deque are decreasing.
invariant.why: A later start with a smaller or equal prefix gives a larger sum AND a shorter subarray.

time.why: Each index enters and leaves the deque once.

space.why: The prefix array and the deque.

wrong: Sliding window needs k to be even.
The window would need a fixed size.

approach: Build prefix P. For each j: while the deque is non-empty and P[j] − P[front] ≥ k, record j − front and pop the front; while P[back] ≥ P[j] pop the back; push j.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
statement: Given an integer array (values may be negative) and an integer k, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k.

nearMiss.why: Negative values break the window: shrinking doesn't reliably lower the sum, so you can't decide when to move left.
The array is not sorted, and subarrays are contiguous ranges, not pairs to converge on.
Kadane finds the maximum sum, not how many subarrays hit an exact value.

trigger.why: An exact subarray-sum target, with negatives allowed: sum(i..j) = P[j] − P[i], so look up P − k in a map.

ds.answer: HashMap<Integer, Integer> prefix sum → count, seeded with {0: 1}

wrong.why: A set loses how many times a prefix occurred, so counts come out too low.

wrong: int[] prefix array with two nested loops
ds.why: Each earlier prefix equal to sum − k is one subarray ending here.

invariant.answer: Before processing index i, the map counts every prefix sum of nums[0..j) for j ≤ i.
wrong: The map only holds prefix sums smaller than k.
The map holds each element's value and index.
invariant.why: So map[sum − k] is exactly the number of valid starts for subarrays ending at i.

time.why: One pass with O(1) map operations.

space.why: Up to n distinct prefix sums.

wrong: Sliding window can't count subarrays, only find the longest.
Sliding window requires k to be positive.
Sliding window only works on strings.

approach: sum = 0, map {0: 1}. For each x: sum += x; count += map[sum − k]; map[sum]++.

twists.change: All values are positive, and you want the shortest subarray reaching the target.
twists.statement: Given an array of positive integers and a target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target, or 0 if none exists.
twists.ds: Two int indices and a running int sum

nearMiss.why: Prefix sums + a map count exact sums when negatives exist; with positives only, the window sum grows and shrinks monotonically, so no map is needed.
A deque over prefix sums is needed when values can be negative (Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K); positives make a plain window enough.
Binary-searching prefix sums per end works in O(n log n), but the window is O(n).

twists.why: Positive values make 'sum ≥ target' monotonic in the window size: expand right, then shrink left while it still holds.
twists.approach: For r: sum += a[r]; while sum ≥ target: best = min(best, r − l + 1); sum −= a[l++]. Return best or 0.

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Return an array where each position holds the product of every other element of the input. You may not use division, and the solution must run in O(n).

nearMiss.why: Kadane keeps a best running value; here every position needs the full product on both its left and its right.
No lookups are needed; each answer is a left product times a right product.
There is no next-greater relationship; every element contributes to every other answer.

trigger.why: Without division, split 'everything except i' into 'everything left of i' × 'everything right of i': prefix and suffix products.

ds.answer: The output int[] filled with left products, then multiplied by a running right product

wrong.t: One long total product, then divide by each element
wrong.why: Division is forbidden, and zeros break it anyway.

ds.why: Reusing the output array keeps extra space O(1).

invariant.answer: After the left pass, answer[i] = product of nums[0..i); during the right pass, right = product of nums(i..n).
wrong: answer is sorted after the first pass.
right holds the product of the whole array.
invariant.why: Multiplying the two gives the product of everything except index i.

time.why: Two linear passes.

space.answer: O(1) extra (the output array isn't counted)

wrong.t: O(n) for separate left and right arrays
wrong.why: That version works, but the follow-up asks for O(1) extra by reusing the output.

space.why: One running variable besides the output.

approach: answer[i] = product of everything to the left (one pass). Then sweep from the right with a running product, multiplying it into answer[i].

title: Continuous Subarray Sum
statement: Given an integer array and an integer k, return true if there is a contiguous subarray of length at least 2 whose sum is a multiple of k.

nearMiss.why: 'Multiple of k' isn't monotonic in window size: growing the window can fix or break it.
A map of element values doesn't help; what repeats is the PREFIX sum modulo k.
No per-position recurrence is needed; two prefix sums with equal remainders already prove a multiple.

trigger.why: A multiple of k ⇒ two prefix sums with the same remainder mod k. Store the first index of each remainder.

ds.answer: HashMap<Integer, Integer> remainder → earliest index, seeded with {0: −1}
ds.why: The earliest index maximises length, which matters for the 'at least 2' rule.

invariant.answer: The map stores the EARLIEST index at which each prefix-sum remainder mod k appeared.
wrong: The map stores the latest index for each remainder.
The running sum is always less than k.
The map holds each element modulo k.
invariant.why: Overwriting with later indices would shorten subarrays and miss valid length-2+ answers.

time.why: One pass.

space.why: At most k remainders, and at most n entries.

wrong: Sliding window can't return a boolean.
Sliding window only works if k is even.
The window would need to be exactly size k.

approach: map {0: −1}. Keep the running sum mod k; if the remainder was seen at index j and i − j ≥ 2 return true; otherwise record only the first index.

title: Maximum Subarray
statement: Given an integer array (negative values possible), find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum.

nearMiss.why: There is no constraint to shrink against; a window can't tell when to drop its left part without Kadane's 'restart' rule.
There is no pair condition and no sorted order to converge on.
One index suffices: the best sum ending at i depends only on the best ending at i − 1.

trigger.answer: contiguous subarray with the largest sum
trigger.why: Maximum-sum contiguous run → at each index, extend the previous run or restart (Kadane).

ds.answer: Two int variables: current run sum and best so far
wrong: int[n][n] table of all subarray sums
ds.why: Only the previous index's value is needed.

invariant.answer: cur is the best sum of a subarray that ends exactly at the current index.
wrong: best is the sum of all positive numbers.
cur resets to 0 whenever a negative number appears.
invariant.why: best is then the max of cur over all indices.

time.why: One pass.

space.why: Two variables.

wrong: Sliding window only finds the longest subarray, never the largest sum.
Sliding window needs the window size to be given.
A window would need the array sorted first.

approach: cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur).

twists.change: The subarray may be at most k elements long.
twists.statement: Given an integer array (values may be negative) and an integer k, return the largest sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray whose length is at most k.
twists.trigger: whose length is at most k
twists.ds: long[] prefix sums and ArrayDeque<Integer> of indices with increasing prefix values

nearMiss.why: Kadane's reset rule has no notion of length; it can't drop elements that fall more than k back.
With negative values there's no rule for when to shrink: a bigger window can be better or worse.
Prefix sums turn it into P[j] − min(P[i]) over j − k ≤ i < j, but that sliding minimum is what the deque provides.

twists.why: Best sum ending at j = P[j] − (minimum prefix in the last k positions) ⇒ sliding-window minimum ⇒ monotonic deque.
twists.approach: Deque holds indices with increasing P. For j: drop front if < j − k; best = max(best, P[j] − P[front]); pop back while P[back] ≥ P[j]; push j.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement: Given daily stock prices, choose one day to buy and a later day to sell to maximise profit. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible.

nearMiss.why: Max minus min over all days ignores that the buy must come before the sell.
Next-greater per day isn't needed; only the minimum price before each day matters.
There's no second sequence or grid; one running minimum is enough.

wrong: or 0 if no profit is possible
trigger.why: The sell must come after the buy, so at each day the best buy is the minimum price SO FAR: a running-best scan.

ds.answer: Two ints: minimum price so far and best profit
ds.why: Nothing else is needed.

invariant.answer: minPrice is the lowest price on any day up to today, so price − minPrice is the best profit if you sell today.
wrong: minPrice is the lowest price over all days.
profit only increases when the price increases.
minPrice is always the first day's price.
invariant.why: best is the max of that over all days.

time.why: One pass.

space.why: Two variables.

wrong: A heap can't hold duplicate prices.
A heap only works when k is given.
A heap gives the max profit only on sorted prices.

approach: Track the minimum price so far; profit = max(profit, price − minPrice).

twists.change: You may now make up to two transactions.
twists.statement: Given daily stock prices, return the maximum profit with at most two buy-then-sell transactions (sell before buying again).
twists.ds: Four ints: buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2

nearMiss.why: Running min price handles one transaction; two need separate states that chain the first sale into the second purchase.
Summing every rise allows unlimited transactions, which can exceed the limit of two.
No single pair of days answers it.

twists.why: A fixed number of steps ⇒ one state per step, updated daily.
twists.approach: buy1 = max(buy1, −p); sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p); buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 − p); sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p).

title: Maximum Product Subarray
statement: Given an integer array that can contain negatives and zeros, return the largest product of any contiguous subarray.

nearMiss.why: Products aren't monotonic with negatives: one more negative can flip the smallest product into the largest.
Prefix products break at zeros and you'd still need the best pair; tracking a running max and min handles signs in one pass.
No two-index state is needed; the best product ending at i depends only on i − 1.

trigger.answer: largest product of any contiguous subarray
trigger.why: Best contiguous run → Kadane; the product twist means tracking the min too, because a negative swaps them.

ds.answer: Three ints: current max, current min, best
ds.why: Both extremes ending at the previous index are enough.

invariant.answer: curMax and curMin are the largest and smallest products of a subarray ending at the current index.
wrong: curMin is always the smallest element seen.
best equals the product of all non-zero elements.
invariant.why: Multiplying by a negative turns the smallest into the largest, so both are kept.

time.why: One pass.

space.why: Three variables.

wrong: A window needs a fixed size k.
Sliding window needs the array sorted.

approach: For each x: if x < 0 swap curMax and curMin; curMax = max(x, curMax · x); curMin = min(x, curMin · x); best = max(best, curMax).

title: Valid Anagram
statement: Given two strings s and t of lowercase English letters, return true if t uses exactly the same letters as s with the same multiplicities (an anagram), otherwise false.

nearMiss.why: There is no window to slide: the whole of t is compared with the whole of s, once.
Sorting both strings and walking them together works, but costs O(n log n); counting is O(n).
XOR of all characters of s and t is 0 for "aa" vs "bb" too, so it can't prove equal multiplicities.

trigger.answer: the same letters as s with the same multiplicities
trigger.why: 'Same items, same counts, order ignored' is a frequency-table comparison.

ds.answer: int[26] counts (increment for s, decrement for t)
wrong: char[] sorted copies of both strings
ds.why: Lowercase letters only ⇒ a fixed 26-slot array beats a HashMap.

invariant.answer: After processing both strings, count[c] = (occurrences in s) − (occurrences in t); all zero ⇔ anagram.
wrong: count[c] is never negative while scanning.
The two strings agree at every index.
A HashSet of s's letters equals a HashSet of t's letters ⇒ anagram.
invariant.why: Sets lose multiplicity ("aab" vs "abb"); a signed count keeps it.

time.why: One pass over each string, then 26 checks.

space.why: The alphabet size is fixed.

wrong: A sliding window can't handle two strings at once.
Sliding windows need a sorted input.
A sliding window would be O(n²) here.

approach: If lengths differ return false. count[s[i] − 'a']++, count[t[i] − 'a']−−; return true iff every count is 0. (Unicode follow-up: HashMap<Character, Integer>.)

twists.change: Find every anagram of a pattern inside a longer string.
twists.statement: Given strings s and p, return every start index in s where a substring of length |p| is an anagram of p.
twists.ds: Two int[26] counts updated as a fixed window slides

nearMiss.why: Counting each substring from scratch is O(|s| · |p|); the window updates one letter in and one out.
Converging ends don't define a fixed-length substring.
Generating permutations of p is factorial.

twists.why: Fixed-length contiguous substrings compared by letter counts ⇒ fixed-size sliding window.
twists.approach: Count p. Slide a window of |p| over s, adding s[r] and removing s[r − |p|]; record r − |p| + 1 when counts match.

title: Majority Element
statement: Given an integer array of length n, return the value that occurs more than n / 2 times. Such a value is guaranteed to exist.

nearMiss.why: A heap over the counts finds the most frequent value, but the > n/2 guarantee means one count pass (or one vote pass) already answers it: no ordering needed.
Occurrences are scattered across the array, not in one contiguous run.
There is no best contiguous subarray to maximise. (Boyer–Moore voting does keep a running counter, but it is a cancellation argument, not a max-subarray recurrence.)

wrong: an integer array of length n
trigger.why: Counting occurrences per value is the direct O(n) solution; the > n/2 guarantee also enables Boyer–Moore voting in O(1) space.

ds.answer: HashMap<Integer, Integer> value → count
ds.why: Counts per value; return as soon as a count passes n / 2.

invariant.answer: count.get(v) is the number of times v has appeared so far; the first value to exceed n / 2 is the answer.
wrong: The majority value is always at index 0 or n − 1.
Counts only ever increase for the current maximum.
The map never holds more than two keys.
invariant.why: With voting instead: pairing off different values never removes all copies of the majority, so the surviving candidate is it.

time.why: One pass. (Sorting and taking nums[n/2] is O(n log n).)

space.answer: O(n) for the map (O(1) with Boyer–Moore voting)
space.why: Up to n/2 distinct keys in the map; voting keeps two scalars.

wrong: A heap can't store duplicate values.
Heaps only work on sorted arrays.
A heap would give the least frequent value.

approach: Count with a HashMap and return the value whose count exceeds n / 2. O(1)-space follow-up: Boyer–Moore: candidate/count; count == 0 ⇒ take the current value; same ⇒ +1, different ⇒ −1.

title: Valid Sudoku
statement: A partially filled 9 × 9 board holds digits 1–9 or '.'. Decide whether the filled cells break any rule: no digit may repeat within a row, within a column, or within any of the nine 3 × 3 boxes. The board does not have to be solvable.

nearMiss.why: Backtracking would SOLVE the puzzle; here we only check the given digits, and solvability is explicitly not required.
There is no in-place traversal trick (rotation, spiral, markers); the work is duplicate detection per group.
A 9-bit mask per row/column/box is a valid speed-up of the same idea, but it is still 'have I seen this digit in this group?': a set.

trigger.answer: no digit may repeat within a row, within a column, or within any of the nine 3 × 3 boxes
wrong: The board does not have to be solvable
trigger.why: 'No repeats within each group' is seen-before detection: one set per group.

ds.answer: boolean[9][9] (or HashSet<Integer>) per row, per column and per box
wrong: HashMap<Integer, List<int[]>> digit → positions, checked pairwise
ds.why: 27 small sets; box index = (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3.

invariant.answer: After scanning a cell, each set holds exactly the digits already seen in that cell's row, column and box; a repeat is found the moment it is added twice.
wrong: Every row contains each digit exactly once.
Empty cells are filled before checking.
Boxes only need checking if rows and columns pass.
invariant.why: Each filled cell is checked against its three groups in O(1).

time.answer: O(81), i.e. O(1) for a fixed board
time.why: Each cell is visited once.

space.why: 27 groups of 9 flags.

wrong: Backtracking would need the board sorted first.

approach: For each filled cell (r, c, d): box = (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3; if row[r][d], col[c][d] or box[box][d] is already set, return false; otherwise set all three.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
statement: An integer array is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the 1-based indices of the two numbers that add up to target (exactly one solution exists), using only constant extra space.

nearMiss.why: A HashMap complement lookup works but uses O(n) space, which the problem forbids.
The two numbers needn't be adjacent or contiguous; we want a pair, not a window.
There is no range sum here: the target is the sum of exactly two elements.

trigger.why: Sorted + pair sum + O(1) space ⇒ converge from both ends.

ds.answer: Two int indices lo and hi on the array
ds.why: Sorted order lets the sum steer which pointer moves.

invariant.answer: If a solution exists, its indices lie within [lo, hi]: a sum too small means nums[lo] can't pair with anything left, so lo++ (and symmetrically hi−−).
wrong: lo and hi always point at equal values.
invariant.why: Each move discards a value that can't be part of any answer.

time.why: Each step moves one pointer inward.

space.why: Two indices.

wrong: Hashing fails when the array is sorted.
A HashMap lookup is O(n) per query.

approach: lo = 0, hi = n − 1. sum < target ⇒ lo++; sum > target ⇒ hi−−; equal ⇒ return {lo + 1, hi + 1}.

twists.change: The array is no longer sorted, and you must return original indices.
twists.statement: Given an unsorted integer array and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target (exactly one solution exists).

nearMiss.why: Sorting first would scramble the original indices (you'd have to carry them along), and costs O(n log n).
It also needs sorted input.
The pair needn't be adjacent.

twists.why: Unsorted + pair sum ⇒ for each value, check whether its complement was seen.
twists.approach: For i: if map has target − a[i] return {map.get(...), i}; map.put(a[i], i).

title: Valid Palindrome
statement: Given a string, decide whether it reads the same forwards and backwards once you ignore every non-alphanumeric character and treat upper and lower case as equal.

nearMiss.why: Expanding from a centre finds palindromic SUBSTRINGS; here the whole string is checked, so start from the ends.
Pushing half the characters and popping to compare works, but needs O(n) space and knowing the cleaned length first.
Character counts can't see order: "ab" and "ba" have the same counts but only one order is a palindrome check.

trigger.answer: reads the same forwards and backwards
wrong: upper and lower case as equal
trigger.why: Whole-string palindrome check ⇒ two pointers from both ends, skipping junk in place.

ds.answer: Two int indices; Character.isLetterOrDigit and Character.toLowerCase
wrong: StringBuilder of the cleaned string, reversed and compared
ds.why: Skipping in place avoids building a cleaned copy (which would be O(n) space).

invariant.answer: Every alphanumeric pair outside [lo, hi] has already matched, case-insensitively.
wrong: lo and hi always point at letters.
The cleaned string has even length.
Characters between lo and hi are already validated.
invariant.why: Mismatch anywhere ⇒ false; pointers crossing ⇒ true.

time.why: Each index is visited once.

space.why: Two indices, no cleaned copy.

wrong: Expanding from the centre is O(n³).
Expand-around-centre only works for odd lengths.

approach: lo = 0, hi = n − 1. Advance lo / retreat hi past non-alphanumerics; compare lowercased chars; mismatch ⇒ false; move both inward.

twists.change: Find the longest palindromic piece instead of checking the whole string.
twists.statement: Given a string, return the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards.
twists.ds: Two int indices per centre (2n − 1 centres)

nearMiss.why: Ends-inward works to check one known string; here the palindrome's position is unknown, so grow outward from every centre.
Being a palindrome isn't monotonic in window size.
Pushing and popping halves needs the centre in advance.

twists.why: Every palindrome has a centre (a character or a gap) ⇒ expand from each.
twists.approach: For each centre expand while s[l] == s[r]; keep the longest.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
statement: An integer array is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove the duplicates in place so each distinct value appears once at the front, keeping their order, and return how many distinct values there are. Use O(1) extra memory.

nearMiss.why: A HashSet of seen values works for unsorted input, but costs O(n) memory; sorted order makes 'new value?' a comparison with the last kept one.
Nothing is measured over a window; one pointer reads, one writes.
Values are not bounded to 1..n, so there is no home index to swap into.

trigger.why: In-place compaction ⇒ read pointer / write pointer (same direction).

ds.answer: Two int indices: read and write
ds.why: The array itself is the output buffer.

invariant.answer: nums[0..write) holds the distinct values seen so far, in order, and nums[write − 1] is the largest of them.
wrong: write and read are always equal.
Every value after write is a duplicate of nums[0].
invariant.why: Because input is sorted, a new value is exactly nums[read] != nums[write − 1].

wrong: O(k · n) for k distinct values
time.why: One pass.

space.why: Two indices.

wrong: Hashing would lose the sorted order of the values.
A HashSet would be O(n²) on sorted input.

approach: write = 1; for read in 1..n−1: if nums[read] != nums[write − 1], nums[write++] = nums[read]. Return write.

twists.change: The array is unsorted; keep the first occurrence of each value, in order.
twists.statement: Given an unsorted integer array, keep only the first occurrence of each value, preserving their order, and return how many values remain at the front.
twists.ds: HashSet<Integer> of seen values plus a write index

nearMiss.why: Comparing with the last kept value only works when equal values are adjacent, i.e. sorted.
Duplicates can be far apart; no window captures them.
Values aren't bounded to 1..n, so there's no home index to mark.

twists.why: Unsorted ⇒ 'have I seen this value?' needs a set.
twists.approach: For each x: if seen.add(x), a[write++] = x. Return write.

title: Merge Sorted Array
statement: nums1 has length m + n: its first m values are sorted and the last n slots are empty padding. nums2 holds n sorted values. Merge nums2 into nums1 so that nums1 ends up fully sorted, writing in place.

nearMiss.why: With only two lists, a heap is overkill: comparing the two current tails is already O(1) per step.
These are single values, not ranges; there is nothing to overlap or sweep.
Partitioning splits around a pivot; here both halves are already sorted and just need interleaving.

trigger.answer: the last n slots are empty padding
trigger.why: Free space at the END ⇒ merge from the back so nothing unread is overwritten.

ds.answer: Three int indices: i = m − 1, j = n − 1, write = m + n − 1
wrong: int[] copy of nums1, merged forwards
ds.why: Writing from the back means no copy is needed.

invariant.answer: nums1[write + 1..] holds the largest values seen so far in sorted order, and write ≥ i, so unread nums1 values are never overwritten.
wrong: i and j always move together.
nums1[0..i] is already in its final place at every step.
invariant.why: write = i + j + 1, so it never passes i.

time.why: Each value is placed once.

space.why: Three indices.

wrong: A heap can't hold duplicate values.
k-way merge needs at least three lists to be correct.
A heap would produce a descending order.

approach: While j ≥ 0: if i ≥ 0 and nums1[i] > nums2[j], nums1[write−−] = nums1[i−−]; else nums1[write−−] = nums2[j−−].

twists.change: Merge k sorted arrays instead of two.
twists.statement: Given k sorted integer arrays, return one sorted array containing all their values.

nearMiss.why: Two pointers merge two arrays; with k, comparing k heads each step is O(k) per element.
You aren't selecting the top k values; the heap holds one head per array while you stream everything out.
Nothing is split around a pivot.

twists.why: Smallest of k heads repeatedly ⇒ min-heap of size k.
twists.approach: Seed the heap with each array's first value; poll, append, push that array's next value.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
statement: Given an integer array sorted in non-decreasing order that may contain negative numbers, return the squares of its values, also in non-decreasing order, in O(n) time.

nearMiss.why: A heap would sort the squares in O(n log n); the input order already tells us where the biggest squares are.
Binary-searching for the first non-negative then expanding outwards works, but the plain two-ends merge needs no search.
It is a two-way merge of the negative and non-negative halves; a heap adds nothing for two lists.

wrong: return the squares of its values
trigger.why: Negatives make the largest squares sit at BOTH ends ⇒ two pointers from the ends, filling the output from the back.

ds.answer: Two int indices lo / hi plus a result int[] filled from the end
wrong: ArrayDeque<Integer> as a stack of negatives
ds.why: The output array is written largest-first.

invariant.answer: The largest remaining square is at lo or hi; result[write + 1..] already holds the largest squares in order.
wrong: Squares between lo and hi are already sorted.
lo always points at a negative number.
The smallest square is always at index 0 of the input.
invariant.why: |x| is largest at the extremes of a sorted array.

time.why: One pass.

space.why: Only the result array.

wrong: A heap can't hold negative numbers.
A heap would return the squares in random order.

approach: lo = 0, hi = n − 1, write = n − 1. Put the larger of nums[lo]², nums[hi]² at result[write−−] and move that pointer inward.

title: Permutation in String
statement: Given strings s1 and s2 of lowercase letters, return true if some contiguous substring of s2 is a rearrangement of s1 (same letters, same counts).

nearMiss.why: Counting is part of it, but recounting every substring from scratch is O(n · m); the window updates counts in O(1) per step.
Generating all permutations of s1 is factorial; we only need to compare letter counts.
Converging pointers from both ends don't define a fixed-length substring to test.

trigger.answer: some contiguous substring of s2 is a rearrangement of s1
trigger.why: Contiguous + fixed length |s1| + letter counts ⇒ fixed-size sliding window.

ds.answer: Two int[26] counts (or one diff array + a 'matches' counter)
wrong: HashSet<String> of all permutations of s1
ArrayDeque<Character> as a queue of the window
ds.why: Add the entering letter, remove the leaving one: O(1) per slide.

invariant.answer: The window is always exactly |s1| long, and its count array equals s2's letters in that window.
wrong: The window never contains a letter absent from s1.
s1's counts change as the window moves.
invariant.why: Equal counts at any position ⇒ true.

time.why: Each slide is O(1) with a matches counter (O(26) with array compare).

space.why: Fixed alphabet.

wrong: Hashing would need s2 sorted first.
Hashing only works when s1 and s2 are the same length.

approach: Count s1. Slide a window of length |s1| over s2, adding s2[r] and removing s2[r − |s1|]; return true when the counts match (track 'matches' among 26 letters for O(1)).

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
statement: Given a binary array and an integer k, you may flip at most k zeros to ones. Return the length of the longest contiguous run of ones you can end up with.

nearMiss.why: A DP over (index, flips used) is O(n · k); the window keeps 'zeros inside ≤ k' with one counter in O(n).
Flipping zeros greedily from the left doesn't know which run to extend; the window tries every right end.
Prefix counts of zeros plus binary search per end works in O(n log n), but the window is simpler and O(n).

trigger.why: Longest contiguous run with 'at most k bad items' ⇒ variable sliding window with a budget.

ds.answer: Two int indices and an int zeros-in-window counter
wrong: ArrayDeque<Integer> as a stack of runs
ds.why: The array itself plus a counter.

invariant.answer: The window [l, r] contains at most k zeros; when a new zero breaks that, l advances until it holds again.
wrong: The window always starts at a zero.
invariant.why: Any window with ≤ k zeros can be made all ones.

time.why: Each pointer moves forward at most n times.

space.why: Two indices and a counter.

wrong: DP would give the shortest run instead.

approach: For r: if nums[r] == 0, zeros++. While zeros > k: if nums[l] == 0, zeros−−; l++. best = max(best, r − l + 1).

title: Maximum Coins From K Consecutive Bags
statement: Bags sit at every integer position on a very long line. You are given non-overlapping segments [l, r, c]: every bag from l to r holds c coins; all other bags are empty. Choose k consecutive positions to collect from and return the most coins possible.

nearMiss.why: Sorting the segments is the first step, but merging or counting overlaps isn't the question; a k-wide window slides over them.
There is no choice to make per segment: the window is one block of k positions, so there's nothing to combine.
Starting at the richest segment can lose: a slightly poorer area with a wider span of coins may win.

trigger.why: A fixed-width block over a line ⇒ sliding window. The best window always starts at some segment's l or ends at some segment's r, so slide over segments (twice: left-aligned and right-aligned).

ds.answer: Segments sorted by l (Arrays.sort with Comparator.comparingInt), two indices and a long running sum
ds.why: Positions go up to 10⁹, so you can't build an array per position.

invariant.answer: With the window [segments[i].l, segments[i].l + k − 1], the running sum holds coins of all segments fully inside it; only the last one can be partially inside.
wrong: The window always covers whole segments.
The best window always starts at position 0.
Segments inside the window are sorted by coins.
invariant.why: Add the partial overlap of segment j explicitly; then repeat with windows ending at each r (or mirror the coordinates).

time.why: The sort dominates; each sweep is linear.

space.answer: O(1) beyond the sort (O(n) if you mirror into a copy)
space.why: A few indices and a long sum.

wrong: Intervals problems can't have coin values.
Merging intervals needs them to overlap, and these never touch.
Interval sweeps only work for k = 1.

approach: Sort by l. Sweep i over segments as window starts (window = [l_i, l_i + k − 1]); advance j while segment j ends inside, adding full coins; add partial coins of segment j. Repeat on mirrored coordinates (windows ending at each r). Answer = max.

title: Jump Game VI
statement: Start at index 0 of an integer array (values may be negative). From index i you may jump to any index in i + 1..i + k. Your score is the sum of values at every index you land on, including the first and last. Return the maximum score on reaching the last index.

nearMiss.why: It IS a DP (best[i] = nums[i] + max of the previous k), but the plain DP is O(n · k); the deque gives that window max in O(1).
A max-heap of (best, index) with lazy deletion works in O(n log n); the deque is O(n).
Always jumping to the largest next value can walk into a run of very negative numbers.

trigger.why: DP whose transition is 'max over the last k states' ⇒ sliding-window maximum ⇒ monotonic deque.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<Integer> of indices with decreasing best[] values, plus int[] best
wrong: int[][] dp[i][j] for each jump length
ds.why: Front = argmax of the last k bests.

invariant.answer: The deque holds indices from the last k positions, with best[] strictly decreasing front to back; the front is the best predecessor of i.
wrong: The deque holds the k most recent indices in order.
best[] is non-decreasing along the array.
The front index is always i − 1.
invariant.why: Pop front when it falls out of range; pop back while best[back] ≤ best[i].

time.why: Each index enters and leaves the deque once.

space.answer: O(n) for best (O(k) for the deque)
space.why: best[] can be the input array itself.

wrong: DP would need the array sorted.
DP gives the minimum score, not the maximum.

approach: best[0] = nums[0]; deque = [0]. For i: drop front if < i − k; best[i] = nums[i] + best[front]; pop back while best[back] ≤ best[i]; push i. Return best[n − 1].

title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit
statement: Given an integer array and a limit, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray in which the difference between its maximum and its minimum is at most limit.

nearMiss.why: A max-heap and a min-heap give max/min, but evicting arbitrary old elements is O(n) (or lazy, O(n log n)); deques evict from the front in O(1).
Binary search on the length with a fixed-window check works in O(n log n) but isn't needed.
Prefix sums give range sums, not range max/min.

trigger.answer: the difference between its maximum and its minimum
wrong: an integer array and a limit
trigger.why: A window whose validity depends on its running MAX and MIN ⇒ two monotonic deques inside a sliding window.

ds.answer: Two ArrayDeque<Integer>: one decreasing (max at front), one increasing (min at front)
ds.why: TreeMap of counts also works in O(n log n); deques make it O(n).

invariant.answer: maxDeque front is the window's max and minDeque front its min; when max − min > limit, l advances (dropping fronts whose index < l).
wrong: Both deques always hold the same indices.
The min is always at index l.
invariant.why: Each deque is monotonic, so its front is the extreme of the current window.

time.why: Every index is pushed and popped at most once per deque.

space.why: Deques can hold the whole window.

wrong: Heaps would return the window in sorted order, which is too slow.

approach: For r: push nums[r] into both deques (popping back while it breaks monotonicity). While front(max) − front(min) > limit: l++ and drop fronts with index < l. best = max(best, r − l + 1).

title: Contiguous Array
statement: Given a binary array, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray that contains an equal number of 0s and 1s.

nearMiss.why: Validity isn't monotonic: shrinking or growing a balanced window can break and then restore balance, so there's no rule for when to move l.
Moving from both ends can't tell which side to give up.
We want a ZERO balance of maximum length, not a maximum sum.

trigger.why: Treat 0 as −1: 'equal counts' = 'subarray sum 0' = two equal prefix sums. Store the first index of each prefix.

ds.answer: HashMap<Integer, Integer> prefix balance → first index (seed {0: −1})
wrong: ArrayDeque<Integer> as a stack of indices
ds.why: Longest ⇒ remember the FIRST index each balance appeared, not how often.

invariant.answer: first.get(b) is the earliest index where the running balance was b, so i − first.get(b) is the longest balanced subarray ending at i.
wrong: first.get(b) is the latest index with balance b.
The balance equals the number of 1s.
invariant.why: Equal prefix balances ⇒ the part between them sums to 0.

time.why: One pass with O(1) map operations.

space.why: Up to 2n + 1 distinct balances (an int[2n + 1] works too).

wrong: A sliding window can't count zeros.
Sliding windows need positive numbers only, and 0 is not positive.
A sliding window would find the shortest subarray.

approach: balance += (x == 1 ? 1 : −1). If first has balance, best = max(best, i − first.get(balance)); else first.put(balance, i). Seed first.put(0, −1).

title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
statement: Build a class over a fixed integer matrix that answers many queries of the form 'sum of all cells in the rectangle from (r1, c1) to (r2, c2)', each in O(1) time.

nearMiss.why: Building the table uses a 2-D recurrence, but there is no optimisation: it's cumulative sums plus inclusion–exclusion per query.
No in-place traversal trick; the work is precomputation.
It is a class, but its whole content is one prefix table; there is nothing to combine.

wrong: sum of all cells in the rectangle
trigger.why: Immutable data + many range-sum queries in O(1) ⇒ precompute prefix sums (here 2-D with inclusion–exclusion).

ds.answer: int[m + 1][n + 1] prefix table P
ds.why: One padded row and column remove edge cases.

invariant.answer: P[i][j] is the sum of the rectangle (0, 0)..(i − 1, j − 1); a query is P[r2+1][c2+1] − P[r1][c2+1] − P[r2+1][c1] + P[r1][c1].
wrong: P[i][j] is the sum of row i only.
Each query needs one row scan.
invariant.why: The top-left corner is subtracted twice, so add it back once.

time.answer: O(m · n) to build, O(1) per query
time.why: Four lookups per query.

space.why: The prefix table.

wrong: 2-D DP would take O(m · n) per query by definition.

approach: P[i+1][j+1] = matrix[i][j] + P[i][j+1] + P[i+1][j] − P[i][j]. Answer queries with inclusion–exclusion.

title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
statement: Given a circular integer array (the end wraps to the start), return the largest possible sum of a non-empty subarray. A subarray may wrap around but may not use any element twice.

nearMiss.why: Doubling the array and using prefix sums with a deque works in O(n), but it is heavier than running Kadane twice.
Prefix sums alone give range sums, not the best range without an extra structure.
With negative values, there's no rule for shrinking the window.

wrong: may not use any element twice
trigger.why: A wrapping subarray = total − (a minimum non-wrapping subarray). So: max Kadane, min Kadane, answer = max(maxSub, total − minSub) unless all are negative.

ds.answer: Scalars: curMax, bestMax, curMin, bestMin, total
wrong: ArrayDeque<Integer> of prefix indices over a doubled array
ds.why: Two Kadane passes in one loop.

invariant.answer: curMax is the best sum ending here; curMin is the worst sum ending here; a wrapping answer is total − bestMin.
wrong: curMin never goes below the smallest element.
invariant.why: Edge case: if bestMax < 0 every element is negative, and total − bestMin would be the empty subarray, so return bestMax.

time.why: One pass.

space.why: Five scalars.

wrong: A deque can't hold negative numbers.

approach: Run Kadane for max and min together, track total. If bestMax < 0 return bestMax; else return max(bestMax, total − bestMin).
